summary: Adds a new signing algorithm, Ed25519-SHA256, to DKIM signatures as defined in RFC 6376. DKIM verifiers are required to implement it.

eli5.summary: Email carries a signature to prove who sent it. This adds a newer, faster kind of pen for signing.

subtitle: Adds Ed25519-SHA256 to DKIM: a signature scheme with much shorter keys than RSA, which every verifier must support.

tldr.problem: DKIM, the system that signs email, defined only one signing algorithm, RSA, which has long keys that are awkward to publish in DNS.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8463 adds Ed25519-SHA256: the usual DKIM message hash is computed with SHA-256 and signed with the Ed25519 variant of EdDSA. The key record in DNS says k=ed25519.
tldr.outcome: Verifiers MUST implement the new algorithm and signers SHOULD. Signers can attach both an RSA and an Ed25519 signature to the same message during the transition.

today: RFC 8463 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 6376 and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Why DKIM Needed a Second Algorithm
sections.content:
DKIM (RFC 6376) signs email by hashing selected header fields and the body, then signing the header hash with a digital signature. Recipients fetch the key needed to check the signature from the DNS.

The original DKIM documents specify a single signing algorithm, RSA. This document adds a second, stronger one: the Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm using the Curve25519 curve, called Ed25519. The RFC notes that it has much shorter keys than RSA for similar levels of security.
sections.eli5: DKIM is a seal on a letter that shows who wrote it. There was only one kind of seal, and it was big. Now there is a second, smaller kind.

sections.title: The Ed25519-SHA256 Algorithm
sections.content:
The new algorithm computes the message hash exactly as Section 3 of RFC 6376 says, using SHA-256 as the hash. It then signs that hash with PureEdDSA, specifically the Ed25519 variant defined in Section 5.1 of RFC 8032.

The DNS record that holds the public key carries the tag k=ed25519, which tells a verifier that the key is an Ed25519 key and not an RSA key. This is the additional signature algorithm that Section 3.3.4 of RFC 6376 had anticipated.

A practical benefit: an Ed25519 public key is 256 bits long, so its base64 form is only 44 octets. The key record will generally fit in a single 255-byte TXT string and work even with DNS provisioning software that does not handle multistring TXT records.
sections.eli5: The message is boiled down to a short fingerprint, and the fingerprint is signed with the new pen. A note in the phone book says which kind of pen was used.

sections.title: Signature and Key Syntax
sections.content:
Two small grammar changes make the new algorithm legal in DKIM. In the signature, the algorithm tag (a=) may now be ed25519: the RFC adds sig-a-tag-k =/ "ed25519" to the ABNF in Section 3.5 of RFC 6376.

In the key record, the key type tag (k=) may now be ed25519, by adding key-k-tag-type =/ "ed25519" to Section 3.6.1 of RFC 6376. The p= value is then the Ed25519 public key encoded in base64, which is 44 octets of text.
sections.eli5: The rule book for writing signatures gets one new word it is allowed to use, and so does the rule book for writing keys.

sections.title: Who Must Implement It
sections.content:
This RFC updates Section 3.3 of RFC 6376 with a single requirement: signers SHOULD implement, and verifiers MUST implement, the Ed25519-SHA256 algorithm.

The asymmetry is deliberate. A verifier has to be able to check any signature it meets, while a signer is only recommended to start producing the new kind.
sections.eli5: Everyone who checks the seals must learn to read the new one. People who make seals are only encouraged to use it.

sections.title: Transition: Signing Twice
sections.content:
For backward compatibility, a signer can add several signatures to one message, some using the old algorithm and some the new one. There can be only a single key record in the DNS for each selector, so the two signatures have to use different selectors, although they can use the same d= and i= identifiers.

The example message in the appendix does exactly this: two signatures with the same d= and i= but different a= algorithms and s= selectors.
sections.eli5: While people switch pens, you can sign the letter twice, once with each pen. Each pen needs its own name tag so the phone book can tell them apart.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
All the security advice in RFC 6376 continues to apply. The one exception is that the advice about Ed25519 in Section 8 of RFC 8032 replaces the advice about RSA threats.

IANA added one value to the "DKIM Key Type" registry: type ed25519, referencing RFC 8032, with status active.
sections.eli5: The old safety rules still count, except that the worries about the old pen are replaced by the worries about the new pen. The new pen's name is written in the official list of pens.

sections.title: A Signed Example Message
sections.content:
The appendix shows a small message from football.example.com carrying both an RSA-SHA256 and an Ed25519-SHA256 signature. The two signatures are independent, so either would be valid if the other were absent. The Ed25519 keys are the test keys from Section 7.1, Test 1, of RFC 8032, converted from hex to base64.

The Ed25519 key record lives at brisbane._domainkey.football.example.com and the RSA one at test._domainkey.football.example.com, so the two selectors are brisbane and test.
sections.eli5: The appendix shows a real-looking letter with two seals on it, each with its own name tag, so you can see how it is done.
